headline: 71.6°F on the Bight Buoy — The Number That Sent Us Looking for the Hudson Wall
subhead: A four-to-six-degree break riding the 100-fathom curve turned a scattered week into a real yellowfin and mahi bite, with bigeye showing after dark.
body_markdown:
71.6°F. That's what buoy 44025 was reading in the NY Bight on the 14th, with seas at 3.3 feet on a 4.0-second period — short, wind-driven chop, not a clean groundswell. That period tells you as much as the temperature does. A 4-second interval means local wind is still stacking the water, which usually means the inshore green stuff hasn't settled and pushed offshore yet. But 71.6 in the Bight in mid-July isn't unusual — what matters is what's happening 60 to 90 miles east of that buoy, out where the canyon wall breaks the shelf.

We ran out of Manasquan Wednesday and picked up a temperature jump crossing the 100-fathom curve — roughly four to six degrees colder-to-warmer depending on which side of the eddy you hit, going from a milky, plankton-thick 68-ish degree shelf water into cleaner blue pushing low-to-mid 70s along the canyon's edge. That's the signature I look for every July: warm core water advecting up from the south, riding the canyon's eastern wall, and shoving the shelf water into a hard edge instead of a gradual fade. When you can see that edge as a color change — green to blue in the space of a quarter mile — you fish it, not the water on either side of it.

The yellowfin have been sitting right on that seam, mostly working the drop from the Dip out toward the Claw, which this week meant trolling water between 39°38'N and 39°44'N along the eastern edge, working depths from 600 to 1,200 fathoms just off the wall. Spread was small skirted ballyhoo and a couple of green machines run tight to the boat, 6 to 7 knots, and the bite window was tight — the first two hours of light and again the last hour before sundown, with almost nothing in the middle of the day. Fish have been running 40 to low 70s in the yellowfin class, nothing giant, but a solid grade for mid-July. I'll be honest, it wasn't a rain of fish — we worked three trolling passes across the temp break Wednesday before we got the spread , and one of our three trips out this week came back with just two fish in the box. That's the canyon in summer: the temperature break tells you where to be, but you still have to find the bait holding on it.

And the bait's there. Squid — mostly shortfin — have been thick on the meter in 40 to 60 fathoms overnight, which is exactly what's pulling the bigeye up off bottom after dark. We've had two solid drops on the chunk right around the Dip between midnight and 3 a.m., butterfish chunks fished slow on circle hooks in 900 to 1,100 feet, bigeye coming up shallower than you'd expect this time of year — call it 200 to 300 feet down on the sounder. That squid show is the same pattern showing up from the Jersey canyons on down through the mid-Atlantic right now, and it's a good sign for the next few weeks because bigeye don't leave a squid buffet in a hurry.

Mahi have been the bright spot for anybody who doesn't want to run all the way to the wall. Any bit of floating structure or a weedline sitting on that same warm-water push has had fish under it — we found a nice mat of sargassum drifting off the Texas Tower grounds Sunday holding gaffer-class mahi to 15 pounds, plus a pile of schoolies that kept the rods bent for twenty minutes on bucktails and small stickbaits. If you're running shorter and don't want to burn the fuel to the canyon proper, working the temp break closer to the Tower with your eyes open for birds and debris is the play — mahi don't care how far offshore they are as long as the water's clean and there's something to hide under.

Wahoo have been a bycatch story more than a target this week — one solid fish taken on a high-speed lure run at 14 knots along the canyon edge while we were repositioning between trolling passes, nothing consistent enough to call a pattern yet. White marlin activity has been light — a couple of raised fish on the troll near the Claw but no real conversions, which tracks with where we are in the season. That usually turns on as the water stabilizes into August.

Looking ahead: if that warm core eddy holds its position on the eastern wall through the weekend — and the short-period chop we've been getting settles into a cleaner groundswell — I'd expect the yellowfin bite to tighten up rather than spread out, concentrating right on that temperature seam between the Dip and the Claw. If the eddy slides east like these things sometimes do in late July, I'd shift effort south toward the Tower grounds and work the mahi under any structure holding on the break. Either way, the squid show at night is the thing to watch — as long as that holds on the meter, the bigeye bite after dark is worth staying out for, even on a night when the troll bite up top goes quiet.
